results.title: Schur triangularization, real Schur form and Schur's inequality
results.informal: Every $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ is $A=UTU^*$ with $U$ unitary and $T$ upper triangular, the eigenvalues on the diagonal in any prescribed order; a real $A$ is $A=QTQ^\top$ with $Q$ real orthogonal and $T$ real upper quasitriangular ($1\times1$ and $2\times2$ blocks $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\-b&a\end{pmatrix}$ for conjugate pairs), and $T$ can be taken triangular when all eigenvalues are real. Consequences: Schur's inequality $\sum_i|\lambda_i|^2=\|A\|_F^2-\|N\|_F^2\le\|A\|_F^2$ ($N$ the strictly upper part, equality iff $A$ normal); matrices with distinct eigenvalues are dense; for every $\varepsilon>0$ some similarity makes $A$ triangular with off-diagonal entries at most $\varepsilon$. Pencil version (QZ): $A=VT_AW^*$, $B=VT_BW^*$ simultaneously.
hypotheses: $A\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ (real Schur form) or $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ (complex Schur form)
prescribed ordering of the eigenvalues for the complex form
results.conclusion: $\exists$ orthogonal $Q$ (unitary $U$), quasitriangular (triangular) $T$: $A=QTQ^\top$; $\sum|\lambda_i|^2\le\|A\|_F^2$ with equality iff $A$ is normal

mathlib_prereqs.note: generalized eigenspaces span (abstract triangularizability); no unitary Schur form

results.notes: Consumers: qr-algorithm-convergence (limit is the Schur form), normal-matrices (normal ⇔ triangular Schur factor diagonal), matrix-power-convergence (ρ(A)<1 ⇒ Aᵏ→0 via the ε-triangular form), gmres-diagonalizable / krylov-nonnormal (Henrici departure from normality, field-of-values-def), Krylov f(A)b error bounds for nonnormal A. Prove: deflation by a unit eigenvector plus orthonormal-completion, induction on n; the real form needs one real invariant 2-plane per conjugate pair. QZ (Thm 2.6.1–2.6.2) is a later variant.

results.title: Normal matrices: spectral theorem, real normal form, Fuglede–Putnam
results.informal: $A$ is normal ($AA^*=A^*A$) iff it is unitarily diagonalizable iff $\|A\|_F^2=\sum|\lambda_i|^2$ iff it has an orthonormal eigenbasis; block triangular normal matrices are block diagonal; two normal matrices are unitarily similar iff they have the same eigenvalues. A real normal matrix is real orthogonally similar to a direct sum of $1\times1$ blocks and $2\times2$ blocks $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\-b&a\end{pmatrix}$ (skew-symmetric and orthogonal matrices as special cases). Fuglede–Putnam: for normal $A,B$, $AX=XB\iff A^*X=XB^*$.
hypotheses: $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ with $AA^*=A^*A$ (or real with $AA^\top=A^\top A$)
results.notes: Consumers: gmres-diagonalizable (κ(V)=1 for normal A), field-of-values-def (W(A)=conv σ(A) for normal A), crouzeix-palencia (normal sanity case), polynomial-spectral-bound generalised to normal A (‖p(A)‖=max|p(λ)|). Prove from schur-triangularization: a normal triangular matrix is diagonal (Lem 2.5.2).

results.title: Diagonalizable matrices and eigenvector bases
results.informal: $A$ is diagonalizable if $A=V\Lambda V^{-1}$ with $\Lambda$ diagonal, equivalently it has $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors, equivalently every eigenvalue has equal geometric and algebraic multiplicity (nondefective). $n$ distinct eigenvalues suffice; a direct sum is diagonalizable iff each summand is; two diagonalizations differ by an invertible block-diagonal factor on the eigenspaces. Geometric multiplicity $\ge k$ forces $\lambda$ into the spectrum of every principal submatrix of order $\ge n-k+1$, hence algebraic multiplicity $\ge k$.
hypotheses: $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ (or real $A$ with a complex eigenvector matrix)
results.conclusion: $\exists V$ invertible, $\Lambda$ diagonal with $A=V\Lambda V^{-1}$ ⇔ $n$ independent eigenvectors ⇔ nondefective; distinct eigenvalues ⇒ diagonalizable
results.notes: Consumers: gmres-diagonalizable (whose Mathlib note asks for exactly this predicate; currently stated with an explicit V), krylov-nonnormal bounds with κ(V), power-iteration for nonsymmetric A, matrix functions f(A)=V f(Λ)V⁻¹. Mostly a wrapper around Mathlib's semisimplicity; prove.

results.title: Commuting families: common eigenvectors and simultaneous diagonalization / triangularization
results.informal: A commuting family has a common eigenvector (Lem 1.3.19) and is simultaneously unitarily upper triangularizable; a family of diagonalizable (normal) matrices commutes iff it is simultaneously (unitarily) diagonalizable, with any eigenvalue order for one member; real diagonalizable matrices with real eigenvalues need only a real similarity. For commuting $A,B$ the eigenvalues of $A+B$ and $AB$ are $\alpha_i+\beta_i$ and $\alpha_i\beta_i$ for suitable orderings. Simultaneous triangularization by similarity is equivalent to unitary simultaneous triangularization.
hypotheses: $\mathcal F\subseteq\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ a commuting family
for diagonalization: every member diagonalizable (normal for the unitary version)
results.conclusion: $\exists S$ (unitary $U$) with $S^{-1}AS$ diagonal (triangular) for all $A\in\mathcal F$

mathlib_prereqs.decl: simultaneous diagonalization of commuting diagonalizable matrices

results.notes: Consumers: matrix functions of commuting symmetric matrices (Loewner-order arguments, operator-monotone-convex), Kronecker sums (kronecker-spectral eigenvalues of A⊗I+I⊗B), preconditioned iterations with commuting preconditioners. The commuting symmetric real case is in Mathlib and should be cited, not reproved.

results.title: Real matrices similar (unitarily similar) over ℂ are similar (orthogonally similar) over ℝ
aliases: unitarily similar real matrices are orthogonally similar
results.informal: If real families $\{A_\alpha\}$, $\{B_\alpha\}$ satisfy $A_\alpha=SB_\alpha S^{-1}$ for one complex nonsingular $S$, then some real nonsingular $T$ does the same (because some $C+\tau D$ is nonsingular when $S=C+iD$); if the common similarity is unitary, a real orthogonal one exists.
hypotheses: $S\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$ nonsingular (resp. unitary) with $A_\alpha=SB_\alpha S^{-1}$ for all $\alpha$
results.conclusion: $\exists T\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ nonsingular (resp. real orthogonal $Q$) with $A_\alpha=TB_\alpha T^{-1}$ ($=QB_\alpha Q^\top$) for all $\alpha$
results.notes: Consumer: NLAlib's complex-embedding transfers (NLAlib.Matrix.ComplexEmbedding, complex volume sampling, complex Cholesky) when a statement proved over ℂ must be brought back to real orthogonal factors. Prove.

results.title: Left and right eigenvectors: biorthogonality and nonunitary deflation
aliases: spectral projector of a simple eigenvalue
results.informal:
If $Ax=\lambda x$ and $y^*A=\mu y^*$ with $\lambda
e\mu$ then $y^*x=0$. If $y^*x
e0$ for the same $\lambda$ then $A=S([\lambda]\oplus B)S^{-1}$ with $S=[x\ S_1]$ and $S^{-*}e_1=y/(x^*y)$ (and conversely). A simple eigenvalue has $y^*x
e0$; for geometric multiplicity one, simplicity is equivalent to $y^*x
e0$, and $\operatorname{adj}(\lambda I-A)=\gamma xy^*$, $\gamma
e0$. Similarities map right eigenvectors by $S$ and left ones by $S^{-*}$.
results.conclusion: $\lambda\ne\mu\Rightarrow y^*x=0$; $\lambda$ simple $\Rightarrow y^*x\ne0$ and $A\sim[\lambda]\oplus B$ with spectral projector $xy^*/(y^*x)$
results.notes: Consumers: eigenvalue condition numbers 1/|y*x| and first-order perturbation of simple eigenvalues (HJ ch. 6, part 2 of this index), deflation in power-iteration for nonsymmetric A, oblique spectral projectors in Krylov f(A)b analysis. Prove.

results.title: Brauer's theorem: eigenvalues of a rank-one update along an eigenvector
results.informal: If $Ax=\lambda x$, $x\ne0$, and the eigenvalues of $A$ are $\lambda,\lambda_2,\dots,\lambda_n$, then for every $v$ the eigenvalues of $A+xv^*$ are $\lambda+v^*x,\lambda_2,\dots,\lambda_n$.
results.notes: Consumers: deflation steps in power-iteration and subspace-iteration-convergence for the next eigenvalue, PageRank-type damping (eigenvalues of αP+(1−α)ev*), rank-one modifications in Lanczos restarts. Prove via the charpoly computation of Ex 1.2.8.

results.title: Sylvester equation AX − XB = C: unique solvability iff disjoint spectra, and spectral block diagonalization
results.informal: For $A\in\mathbb C^{n\times n}$, $B\in\mathbb C^{m\times m}$ the map $X\mapsto AX-XB$ is invertible iff $\sigma(A)\cap\sigma(B)=\emptyset$ (real data give real solutions); $AX=XB$ implies $g(A)X=Xg(B)$ for all polynomials $g$. Consequences: if $AB=CA$ with block-diagonal $B,C$ whose off-diagonal block spectra are disjoint then $A$ is block diagonal; matrices commuting with $S(A_1\oplus\cdots\oplus A_d)S^{-1}$ (disjoint spectra) are $S(B_1\oplus\cdots\oplus B_d)S^{-1}$; every $A$ is similar to $T_{11}\oplus\cdots\oplus T_{dd}$ with each $T_{ii}$ triangular with a single eigenvalue.

mathlib_prereqs.note: coprimality of the characteristic polynomials gives the Bézout argument

results.notes: Consumers: sylvester-separation-bound (its quantitative symmetric form; this is the qualitative general statement), davis-kahan-sin-theta and wedin-sin-theta (both reduce to a Sylvester equation), spectral projectors and invariant-subspace perturbation for nonsymmetric matrices, block diagonalization used in Krylov f(A)b analysis. Prove via Cayley–Hamilton: p_B(A) is invertible when the spectra are disjoint, which inverts X ↦ AX − XB.

results.title: Convergent and power-bounded matrices: Aᵏ → 0 iff ρ(A) < 1
results.informal: $A^k\to0$ iff $\rho(A)<1$; then $\sum_kA^k=(I-A)^{-1}$. $\sup_k\|A^k\|<\infty$ iff $\rho(A)\le1$ and every eigenvalue of modulus one is semisimple. Quantitatively, for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $C_\varepsilon$ with $\|A^k\|\le C_\varepsilon(\rho(A)+\varepsilon)^k$.
results.conclusion: $\lim_{k\to\infty}A^k=0\iff\rho(A)<1$; power bounded $\iff\rho(A)\le1$ and unimodular eigenvalues semisimple

mathlib_prereqs.note: Gelfand's formula gives the ρ<1 direction quickly

results.notes: Consumers: richardson-iteration and chebyshev-iteration (stationary/polynomial methods converge iff ρ of the iteration matrix < 1), Jacobi/Gauss–Seidel style splittings, expected-error recursions of randomized-kaczmarz and sketch-and-project (E[e_{k+1}] = (I − P̄) E[e_k]), inverse-perturbation (Neumann series beyond the ‖F‖<1 criterion). The convergent part follows from Gelfand's formula in Mathlib; the power-bounded part needs Jordan structure: state it, assume if needed. Also Thm 5.6.12, Cor 5.6.13 (HJ ch. 5 form).

results.title: CS decomposition of a partitioned unitary matrix and canonical form of an oblique projection
aliases: complementary blocks of a unitary have equal rank
results.informal: If $U=\begin{pmatrix}U_{11}&U_{12}\\U_{21}&U_{22}\end{pmatrix}$ is unitary (real orthogonal) with $U_{11}\in\mathbb C^{p\times p}$, $p\le q$, there are unitaries $V_1,W_1\in\mathbb C^{p\times p}$, $V_2,W_2\in\mathbb C^{q\times q}$ with $(V_1\oplus W_1)U(V_2\oplus W_2)=\begin{pmatrix}C&S&0\\-S&C&0\\0&0&I_{q-p}\end{pmatrix}$, $C=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_i(U_{11}))$, $S=(I-C^2)^{1/2}$. In particular $\operatorname{rank}U_{12}=\operatorname{rank}U_{21}$ and $\operatorname{rank}U_{22}=\operatorname{rank}U_{11}+n-2p$. An idempotent $P$ with singular values $\sigma_1\ge\dots\ge\sigma_g>1$ is unitarily similar to $\bigoplus_i\begin{pmatrix}1&(\sigma_i^2-1)^{1/2}\\0&0\end{pmatrix}\oplus I\oplus0$, so $\|P\|=1/\cos\theta_{\max}$ between its range and the orthogonal complement of its null space.
hypotheses: $U\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}$ orthogonal, partitioned with $U_{11}\in\mathbb R^{p\times p}$, $p\le n-p$
results.conclusion: block-orthogonal $V,W$ with $V^\top UW$ in CS form; $\operatorname{rank}U_{12}=\operatorname{rank}U_{21}$; for idempotent $P$, $\|P\|=\sigma_1(P)$ is the secant of the largest principal angle
results.notes: Consumers: principal-angles-def (CSD is the canonical form behind sin Θ/cos Θ; several of its lemmas are currently scaffolds: sinThetaMax_comm, sinThetaMax_eq_sin_principalAngles), davis-kahan-sin-theta, wedin-sin-theta, oblique projectors in Nyström / generalized Nyström and sketch-and-solve-ls analyses (‖P‖ = ‖I − P‖ = 1/cos θ), subspace-iteration-convergence. Prove from svd + qr-decomposition as in HJ's proof.

results.title: Cauchy–Binet formula and multiplicativity of compound matrices
results.informal: For $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times k}$, $B\in\mathbb F^{k\times n}$ and index sets $|\alpha|=|\beta|=r$: $\det(AB)[\alpha,\beta]=\sum_{|\gamma|=r}\det A[\alpha,\gamma]\det B[\gamma,\beta]$; equivalently the $r$-th compound is multiplicative, $C_r(AB)=C_r(A)C_r(B)$. Special case: $\det(A^\top A)=\sum_{|S|=k}\det(A_{S,:})^2$ for $A\in\mathbb R^{m\times k}$.
results.notes: Consumers: volume sampling and DPP normalisers (NLAlib.LowRank.VolumeSampling, complex volume sampling: Σ_S det(A_S A_Sᵀ) = e_k(σ²) currently reached through principal-minor sums of a Gram matrix), leverage-score / projection-DPP identities, the k = rank case of Gram determinants. Prove (standard multilinearity argument) and upstream to Mathlib if possible.

results.title: Rank inequalities (Sylvester, Frobenius, subadditivity) and solvability of linear systems
aliases: rank(AB) ≥ rank A + rank B − n
results.informal: $\operatorname{rank}(A+B)\le\operatorname{rank}A+\operatorname{rank}B$; $\operatorname{rank}A+\operatorname{rank}B-k\le\operatorname{rank}AB\le\min(\operatorname{rank}A,\operatorname{rank}B)$ for $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times k}$, $B\in\mathbb F^{k\times n}$ (Sylvester); $\operatorname{rank}AB+\operatorname{rank}BC\le\operatorname{rank}B+\operatorname{rank}ABC$ (Frobenius). $Ax=b$ is solvable iff $\operatorname{rank}[A\ b]=\operatorname{rank}A$, and the solution set is $x_0+\ker A$.
results.conclusion: Sylvester, Frobenius and subadditivity inequalities for matrix rank; Rouché–Capelli criterion
results.notes: Consumers: sketch rank arguments (ae_rank_mul_gaussian_eq_min, gaussian-sketch range finder: rank(AΩ) ≥ rank A + rank Ω − n), Nyström rank bookkeeping, kaczmarz-rank-deficient (consistency b ∈ range A), sketch-and-solve-ls. Prove; small.

results.title: Law of complementary nullities and Jacobi's identity for minors of the inverse
aliases: rank of off-diagonal blocks of A⁻¹
results.informal: For nonsingular $A$ and index sets $\alpha,\beta$: $\operatorname{nullity}A[\alpha,\beta]=\operatorname{nullity}A^{-1}[\beta^c,\alpha^c]$; $\det A^{-1}[\alpha^c,\beta^c]=(-1)^{p(\alpha,\beta)}\det A[\beta,\alpha]/\det A$. For a $2\times2$ block matrix with nonsingular $A_{11}$, $\operatorname{rank}A=\operatorname{rank}A_{11}+\operatorname{rank}(A_{22}-A_{21}A_{11}^{-1}A_{12})$.
results.notes: Consumers: rank structure of inverses (off-diagonal low rank of inverses of banded/tridiagonal matrices; hierarchical-matrix sketching), Schur-complement rank additivity used by partial-cholesky / randomly pivoted Cholesky residual rank arguments. Low priority.

results.title: Toeplitz, Hankel and Cauchy matrices
results.informal: Toeplitz: $a_{ij}=t_{j-i}$; Hankel: $a_{ij}=h_{i+j}$; Cauchy: $a_{ij}=1/(x_i+y_j)$ with $\det=\prod_{i<j}(x_j-x_i)(y_j-y_i)/\prod_{i,j}(x_i+y_j)$ (Hilbert matrix as a special case). Circulants (in Mathlib) are the Toeplitz matrices that commute with the cyclic shift.
results.conclusion: definitions with the Cauchy determinant formula
results.notes: Consumers: Toeplitz and partial-circulant JL sketches, moment (Hankel) matrices in Lanczos / Gauss quadrature (lanczos-gauss-quadrature, jacobi-matrix-identities), ill-conditioning examples (Hilbert, Cauchy) for condition-number-def. Low priority.

results.title: Jacobi's formula: derivative of the determinant
aliases: d det A = tr(adj A dA)
results.informal: If $t\mapsto A(t)$ is differentiable then $\frac{d}{dt}\det A(t)=\operatorname{tr}(\operatorname{adj}A(t)\,A'(t))$, so $\frac{d}{dt}\log\det A(t)=\operatorname{tr}(A(t)^{-1}A'(t))$ when $\det A(t)>0$. The derivative of $p_A(t)$ is the sum of the principal $(n-1)$-minors of $tI-A$.
results.notes: Consumers: log-determinant estimation (SLQ for tr log A = log det A, slq-error), Gaussian-process likelihood gradients via Hutchinson (hutchinson-variance), concavity of log det (operator-monotone-convex family), NLAlib.hasDerivAt_matrix_inv companions. Prove (multilinearity in the columns).

results.title: Companion matrices, nonderogatory matrices and cyclic vectors
results.informal: The companion matrix $C_p$ of a monic $p$ has $p$ as both minimal and characteristic polynomial. For $A\in\mathbb F^{n\times n}$: $\deg q_A=n$ ⇔ $q_A=p_A$ ⇔ $A$ nonderogatory (every eigenvalue geometrically simple) ⇔ $A$ is similar to $C_{p_A}$ ⇔ some $b$ has Krylov grade $n$; then every matrix commuting with $A$ is a polynomial in $A$.
results.notes: Consumers: krylov-grade (grade ≤ deg q_A with equality for a cyclic vector; the Krylov matrix K satisfies AK = K C), arnoldi-relation (Hessenberg form of A in a Krylov basis is similar to a companion matrix), gmres-any-convergence-curve (construction uses companion matrices). Prove.

results.title: LU factorization of possibly singular matrices: row and column inclusion
results.informal: $A$ has an LU factorization with nonsingular $L$ iff for each $i<n$ the row $A[i+1,1{:}i]$ is a combination of the rows of $A[1{:}i,1{:}i]$ (row inclusion); dually for nonsingular $U$ and column inclusion. If $\operatorname{rank}A=k$ and the leading $j\times j$ blocks are nonsingular for $j\le k$, $A=LU$ with either factor unit triangular.
results.conclusion: $\exists L$ unit lower, $U$ upper with $A=LU$ ⇔ row inclusion; leading blocks nonsingular up to the rank ⇒ LU exists
results.notes: Consumers: partial-cholesky and randomly pivoted Cholesky on rank-deficient PSD matrices (the LDLᵀ analogue), CUR / skeleton decompositions (A = C U⁺ R from a nonsingular leading block). Low priority; NLAlib's lu-decomposition covers the nonsingular case.
